notice.title: History and imagination
notice.text: YUDDH is inspired by real history. Its battles, names and numbers are adapted to make a game, and some stories come from tradition rather than proof. Dates, battle sites, alliances and sequences of events are sometimes uncertain, debated, combined or invented for play, and where the game invents something it says so. Inscriptions and court chronicles show the view of the people who ordered them. Every battle has a History note with its sources, and each victory ends with a short epilogue.
notice.source: Tags: HISTORY (recorded in surviving sources), TRADITION (later stories, or readings historians debate), INVENTED (added by the game).

first_throne.happened: Chandragupta Maurya founded the Maurya dynasty by displacing the Nandas of Magadha, conventionally dated around 322–321 BCE. How he did it is not securely known: the Greek and Roman writers say almost nothing about it, and the dramatic stories come from Indian texts written much later. The Nandas were remembered as rich and powerful; Plutarch repeats reports of a vast army with thousands of elephants, figures no historian trusts.

changed.text: The Nanda dynasty ended and Chandragupta's dynasty ruled Magadha. That change of power is the firm part of the story.
Chanakya (Kautilya) as Chandragupta's adviser comes from later Indian stories. Amatya Rakshasa and Parvataka are characters from the later play Mudrarakshasa, not proven participants.
One battle at the gates of Pataliputra. Its date, site and fighting are not recorded, and the seasons and every card's power are game rules.

first_throne.source: Sources: Plutarch, Life of Alexander 62; Justin 15.4; the Puranas and Buddhist and Jain traditions; Vishakhadatta's Mudrarakshasa (a later drama); Jansari, Chandragupta Maurya (UCL Press).
first_throne.epilogue: Chandragupta held Pataliputra and went on to bring most of the north under one rule. A few years later he would meet the Greek-ruled lands at the Indus.

indus_line.happened: Around 305–303 BCE Seleucus I, one of Alexander's successors, crossed toward the Indus and dealt with Chandragupta until they made an agreement. Ancient writers record its terms: Seleucus gave up some eastern lands, the two courts were joined by a marriage arrangement, and Chandragupta sent 500 war elephants. Which lands, and who had the better of the fighting, nobody knows; no ancient writer shows either king as the clear winner.

changed.text: A treaty with territory, elephants and a marriage tie is recorded by Strabo, Justin and Appian, writing long after the event.
A battle on the Indus with a winner. The sources do not say where the armies met or how the fighting went.
The figure of 500 elephants is the ancient one, and round numbers may be exaggerated. The story of Seleucus's daughter Helena is a later popular addition.
Macedonian pikes (the phalanx), Companion cavalry and Cretan archers are how Hellenistic armies fought. Megasthenes was a Greek envoy at Pataliputra; his Indica survives only in fragments.

indus_line.source: Sources: Strabo 15.2.9; Justin 15.4; Appian, Syrian Wars 55; Plutarch; fragments of Megasthenes; Jansari, Chandragupta Maurya (UCL Press).
indus_line.epilogue: The treaty settled the frontier for a generation. Seleucus turned west, where tradition says his elephants served him at the battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE, and Chandragupta's empire held the north-west.

digvijaya.happened: The Allahabad (Prayaga) Pillar carries a praise-poem for Samudragupta by his court poet Harishena. It names northern kings it says he "uprooted", among them Ganapatinaga, Nagasena and Achyutanandin, and twelve southern kings who were captured and then released and restored. Forest rulers, frontier kingdoms and distant powers are said to have paid tribute or sent envoys. His gold coins show him playing the veena.

changed.text: One battle at Padmavati against three Naga kings together. The pillar names the kings but gives no site, date or account of the fighting. Whether the Nagas fell once or twice is debated.
Poisoned arrows (Sarpa Vish). The cobra is the Naga symbol; the venom is the game's own idea.
The veena coin is real. The pillar is the winner's own account, so the defeated kings' side is missing.

digvijaya.source: Sources: Allahabad (Prayaga) Pillar inscription by Harishena, as edited in Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum vol. III; Gupta lyrist gold coins (Indian Museum, Kolkata).
digvijaya.epilogue: After the north and the south, his gold coins proclaim an Ashvamedha, the horse sacrifice of a sovereign. He did not rule everywhere directly: some kings were removed, some restored, and others only sent tribute and envoys. His son Chandragupta II would carry Gupta power west.

golden_age.happened: Chandragupta II (ruled about 375–415 CE) ended the rule of the Western Kshatrapas, Saka kings who had ruled Malwa, Gujarat and Saurashtra for centuries. A cave inscription at Udayagiri, dated about 401 CE, records his minister travelling with the king as he sought to conquer the whole earth. The Kshatrapa silver coins stop, and Gupta silver coins in the same style appear, around 409 CE. When and where the last fighting happened is not recorded.

changed.text: One battle at Ujjain against Rudrasimha III, and his fall in it. The coins show a change of rule, not a battle; "c. 409 CE" is the coin date, not a battle date.
Vikramaditya and the nine gems (Navaratna), with the poet Kalidasa among them, are a later legend. Historians debate who Vikramaditya was.
The Iron Pillar of Delhi is often linked to Chandragupta II, but its king is only named "Chandra", and nothing says it defended Ujjain.
The desert storm (Marubhumi Toofan) is the game's own.

golden_age.source: Sources: Udayagiri cave inscriptions (Gupta year 82, about 401 CE); Western Kshatrapa and Gupta silver coins; later Sanskrit tradition of Vikramaditya; Delhi Iron Pillar inscription.
golden_age.epilogue: With the west won, Gupta rule reached the Arabian Sea and its trading ports, and its coins carried a new image in a familiar silver style. The Chinese monk Faxian travelled through the empire around these years.
